hook: You know Jesus said he is the way. But did you know he told it to a disciple who said he did not know the way, and that his followers were once called the Way?
story:
Jesus has just told his friends that he is leaving. “Don’t let your heart be troubled,” he says, and then, “You know where I go, and you know the way.”

Thomas will not let that pass. “Lord, we don’t know where you are going. How can we know the way?” It is the honest question of a man who has stopped pretending to understand. We have met him before. When Jesus decided to go back toward Judea, where people had just tried to stone him, it was Thomas who said, “Let’s also go, that we may die with him.” He is not a man who hangs back. He simply says out loud what the others may have been thinking.

Jesus does not answer with directions. He does not point to a road, a rule or a place on the map. He says, “I am the way, the truth, and the life.” The answer to a question about a route is a person. Right after, Philip asks to be shown the Father, and Jesus says, “He who has seen me has seen the Father.”

The words came on the night before Jesus was arrested, to friends who were afraid of losing him. Read there, they are first of all a promise: you are not being left to find the road alone.

moment:
Think of who is at the table. Peter has just asked where Jesus is going and has been told, “Where I am going, you can’t follow now, but you will follow afterwards.” Peter answers that he will lay down his life, and Jesus tells him he will deny him three times. Then Jesus turns to all of them: “Don’t let your heart be troubled. Believe in God. Believe also in me.”

These are the words of a teacher who knows what is about to happen, speaking to friends who do not. He talks about his Father’s house, about preparing a place, about coming again. Thomas and Philip each break in with a plain question, and each time Jesus answers patiently instead of correcting them for asking. Later in the same talk he gives them his peace and says, “Don’t let your heart be troubled, neither let it be fearful.”
around:
Right after the verse, Jesus ties the way to the Father: “If you had known me, you would have known my Father also.” A few verses on he says that the one who loves him will keep his word, and that the Father and Jesus “will come to him and make our home with him.” The picture is of a home and a welcome, not only of a road.

The chapter also promises help for the road: “another Counselor”, the Spirit of truth, who “will teach you all things”. The saying about the way is surrounded by people being given something, not by people being tested.
after:
Thomas did come to know the way he asked about. After the resurrection he was not with the others when Jesus first appeared, and said he would not believe unless he saw “the print of the nails” in Jesus’ hands. A week later Jesus stood among them and invited him to touch his hands. Thomas answered, “My Lord and my God!”

The early believers took the word way as their own name. Saul went looking for anyone “of the Way”, men or women. Later, as Paul, he said he “persecuted this Way to the death”. Standing before a governor he said, “according to the Way, which they call a sect, so I serve the God of our fathers”. We cannot prove that the name comes from this very verse, but the verse is one place where Jesus says it of himself. Another early Christian text, the Didache, opens with two ways, one of life and one of death.

The church history we have for Thomas is partly tradition. Eusebius wrote around 325 that tradition gave Parthia to Thomas, and the 1911 Britannica says the oldest tradition makes him the evangelist of Parthia. A later tradition sends him on to India. The same article records that the oldest surviving tradition says he did not die as a martyr at all. Eusebius also reports that Thomas, under divine impulse, sent Thaddeus to Edessa. The Bible itself does not say where he went.
readings:
Most Christians through the centuries have heard the second half of the verse as a plain statement: “No one comes to the Father, except through me.” They read it as saying that Jesus is the one who opens the way to God. Other New Testament voices say the same in their own words. Hebrews calls it “a new and living way”, and Paul writes that “through him we both have our access in one Spirit to the Father.”

Others stress what kind of statement it is. It is not a boast against anyone, they point out, but a reply to a frightened friend. For them the weight falls on the first half: Jesus does not say he shows the way, he says he is the way, and the Father is where it leads.

A third group wrestles with how far the second half reaches, and what it says about people who have never heard of Jesus. The verse itself does not take up that question. Readers who care about it often turn to the rest of the Bible, and they do not all agree.
point: Taken alone, the verse can sound like a gate with a guard. In its setting it is a hand held out to a worried disciple. Thomas asked for a road, and Jesus gave him himself. The way is a person who goes with you, not a map you have to read alone.
lesson:
If you have ever felt that you do not know the way, in your faith, in your grief or in an ordinary week, notice who Jesus is talking to. He is talking to a man who said it out loud. Nothing in the passage scolds Thomas for not knowing.

You are invited to bring the question the same way. You can say to God that you do not know where you are going, and ask. You could read John 14 slowly, from the first verse to the last, and let the whole chapter answer before you decide what one verse means.

And if you do not share this faith, you can still see what the scene offers. A person who admits he does not know is not turned away in this story. He is given an answer.

echoes.note: The letter speaks of entering God’s presence “by the way which he dedicated for us, a new and living way”. Here too the way is something Jesus opens.
Paul says “through him we both have our access in one Spirit to the Father”. It is the same road to the Father, now said of Jew and non-Jew together.
Long before, a psalmist prayed, “Show me your ways, LORD. Teach me your paths.” Asking God to show the way was already a prayer in Israel.
